**WASHINGTON/ALBANY** — Hillary Rodham Clinton officially resigned her seat in the United States Senate this week, closing an eight-year chapter representing New York and opening one of the most closely watched political sequences in recent state history as Governor David Paterson prepares to name her successor.

## The Resignation

Clinton's departure clears the way for her confirmation as Secretary of State in the incoming administration, a role that will position her as America's chief diplomat after a career that took her from First Lady to U.S. Senator to presidential candidate. Her resignation letter, delivered to New York's Secretary of State as required by law, formally ended a tenure that began in January 2001 when she became the first First Lady to win elected office.

During her time in the Senate, Clinton built a reputation as a policy-focused legislator, serving on the Armed Services Committee and developing relationships across the aisle that many credited with easing her transition into a foreign policy role. Colleagues from both parties offered tributes on the floor, with several noting the historic nature of her career arc.

## The Appointment Power

Under New York law, Governor Paterson holds sole authority to appoint an interim replacement who will serve until a special election can be held, expected in November 2010, with the seat then up for a full term in 2012. The appointee will need to be confirmed by voters in that special election to continue serving.

This appointment power has thrust Paterson into an unusually prominent national spotlight at a moment when his own approval ratings have been under pressure amid New York's fiscal crisis and questions about his leadership following his ascension from the lieutenant governor's office after Eliot Spitzer's resignation.

## The Speculation List

Political insiders and reporters have engaged in weeks of intense speculation over who might receive the appointment. Names floated prominently include:

- **Caroline Kennedy** — The daughter of President John F. Kennedy has actively lobbied for the seat, drawing both intrigue over her family legacy and skepticism about her lack of electoral experience.
- **Andrew Cuomo** — New York's Attorney General, son of former Governor Mario Cuomo, is seen by many as the most politically seasoned option, though some speculate he may prefer to run for governor himself.
- **Kirsten Gillibrand** — A House member from a swing district, seen as a compromise candidate who could balance upstate and downstate political considerations.
- **Nassau County Executive Thomas Suozzi** and several other House members and local officials have also been mentioned as possibilities.

## Political Calculations

Paterson faces a complex set of considerations beyond simple qualification. He must weigh:

**Electability in 2010**: Any appointee will need to run in a special election within roughly two years, meaning fundraising ability and statewide name recognition matter enormously.

**Geographic and Demographic Balance**: New York's political map requires sensitivity to upstate/downstate divides, as well as the state's diverse coalition of voters across New York City boroughs, suburbs, and rural regions.

**Gender Representation**: With Clinton's departure, some Democratic activists have expressed strong interest in Paterson naming another woman to avoid an all-male congressional delegation at the Senate level.

**Personal Political Relationships**: Paterson's own re-election prospects in 2010 could be shaped by his choice — an appointee with strong establishment ties could help or hurt his standing depending on how the decision is perceived by various factions within the party.

**The Kennedy Factor**: The possibility of a Kennedy filling the seat once held by Robert F. Kennedy carries symbolic weight but has also generated pointed questions from editorial boards and rival campaigns about whether name recognition should substitute for a demonstrated record in public service.

## Reaction from Albany and Beyond

Democratic officials in Albany have described the decision-making process as unusually opaque, with Paterson keeping his deliberations close and declining to commit to a timeline beyond suggesting an announcement would come "in due course." Republican officials, watching from the sidelines, have signaled they intend to contest the seat aggressively in 2010 regardless of who is named, viewing an appointed — rather than elected — senator as vulnerable.

National Democratic strategists have also weighed in privately, with some expressing concern that a contentious selection process could create early friction for the incoming administration, particularly given Clinton's continued influence within party circles even as she transitions to the State Department.

## What Comes Next

Paterson is expected to make his selection in the coming weeks, with the successor to be sworn in shortly after Clinton's confirmation as Secretary of State is finalized. Whoever receives the nod will immediately face the dual challenge of governing during a difficult economic period while simultaneously building a campaign operation for a high-profile statewide race just months away.

The decision will be closely scrutinized not only for what it says about New York's political future, but as an early indicator of how Democratic power dynamics will play out heading into the 2010 midterm cycle.

*This story reflects developments as of the transition period following the 2008 presidential election.*

# Clinton Confirmed as Secretary of State After Senate Debate Over Foundation Ties

**WASHINGTON** — The Senate voted overwhelmingly Monday to confirm Hillary Rodham Clinton as the nation's 67th secretary of state, capping weeks of scrutiny over potential conflicts of interest tied to her husband's charitable foundation and the couple's global business relationships.

The vote, 94-2, came after senators on the Foreign Relations Committee pressed Clinton during confirmation hearings last week about how the State Department would navigate the web of foreign government contributions flowing into the William J. Clinton Foundation, established by former President Bill Clinton after he left office in 2001.

Senator Richard Lugar of Indiana, the committee's ranking Republican, had warned that the foundation's fundraising activities "will present numerous opportunities for conflicts of interest, real or apparent," particularly given contributions from foreign governments seeking favor with the incoming administration.

In response to concerns raised during the vetting process, Bill Clinton agreed to a series of unprecedented disclosure arrangements, including the release of a list of roughly 200,000 foundation donors and a pledge to submit future foreign government contributions for ethics review by the State Department while his wife served in her post. He also agreed to step down from an annual meeting tied to his foundation's business initiatives and to forgo new foreign government donations to the foundation altogether during her tenure.

Critics, including some Republican senators, argued the agreement did not go far enough, noting that existing pledges and donations already collected would remain largely shielded from public accounting. Senator John Cornyn of Texas said he remained "concerned that the agreement...does not eliminate the potential appearance of conflicts."

Clinton, in written responses to the committee, defended the arrangement, stating that "the country needs my husband's foundation to continue its work" while emphasizing that safeguards had been put in place "to ensure there is no actual or apparent conflict with my service as secretary of state."

Despite the lingering unease among some lawmakers, the confirmation proceeded with broad bipartisan support, reflecting confidence in Clinton's qualifications following her presidential campaign and eight years in the Senate representing New York. Senators Robert Byrd of West Virginia and Jim DeMint of South Carolina were the two dissenting votes, though DeMint's office said his opposition stemmed principally from concerns over the foundation issue rather than Clinton's qualifications broadly.

President Barack Obama, who nominated Clinton after their hard-fought Democratic primary contest, praised the vote in a statement Monday evening, calling her "a leader of tremendous experience and standing on the world stage" who would help "renew American leadership and diplomacy."

Clinton was expected to be sworn in later this week, becoming the third woman to hold the office of secretary of state, following Madeleine Albright and Condoleezza Rice.

The State Department said the agreement governing foundation disclosures would remain in effect throughout Clinton's tenure, with periodic reviews conducted by the department's ethics office to assess compliance and address any new concerns that arise regarding foreign contributions.
